How do I choose origami paper for different models?
a: Origami paper comes in a wide variety of types, each suited to different models and skill levels. Kami (standard origami paper) is the most common—thin, crisp, colored on one side and white on the other, ideal for beginner to intermediate models. Foil paper has a thin metal layer bonded to paper, holding sharp creases and resisting fraying, making it excellent for complex models with many layers but difficult to shape sculpturally. Tissue foil laminates tissue paper to aluminum foil, combining the foldability and thinness of tissue with the memory of metal, and is the preferred paper for super-complex designs like Kamiya's dragons. Tant paper is a dense, evenly colored paper with a smooth matte finish that works beautifully for modular origami and geometric forms, while washi, traditional Japanese handmade paper made from kozo, mitsumata, or gampi fibers, is prized for its texture, durability, and natural elegance in display pieces.

What size origami paper do professionals use?
a: The standard size for origami paper is 15cm x 15cm (about 6 inches square), which is suitable for most models and easy for beginners to handle. Larger sizes—24cm, 35cm, or even 50cm and above—are used for complex models with many steps because they provide more working area for layers and details, while miniature folding uses squares as small as 2.5cm or 1cm for micro-origami. To cut square paper from rectangular sheets (such as letter or A4), fold the sheet diagonally to align the short edge with the long edge and trim the excess rectangle, or use a paper cutter, rotary cutter, or sharp craft knife with a metal ruler and cutting mat for precise results. Professional folders often invest in specialty papers in custom sizes and maintain a collection of squares ranging from 10cm for simple models to 70cm+ for super-complex multi-session projects.

What workspace is best for origami?
a: Traditional origami philosophy holds that no tools beyond paper and hands are necessary, but many folders use simple implements to improve precision. A bone folder or folding bone—a smooth, blunt tool made of bone, plastic, or wood—is used to sharpen creases and flatten layers without marring the paper surface, especially useful for thick papers and complex models with many folded layers. Fine-tipped tweezers help manipulate tiny flaps and make precise adjustments on intricate designs, a paper clip or clothespin can hold layers temporarily during assembly, and a spray bottle is essential for wet folding techniques. For workspace, a large, clean, flat surface with good lighting is critical; many serious folders also use a self-healing cutting mat as a combined work surface and measurement guide, and some use a rotating turntable to examine models from all angles during shaping.
